key_points.text: Exam notation: ∧ (AND, conjunction), ∨ (OR, disjunction), ¬ (NOT, negation), ⊻ (XOR, exclusive disjunction), ≡ (equivalence). You can answer using alternatives: AND or . for ∧; OR or + for ∨; NOT, ~ or an overbar for ¬; XOR or ⊕ for ⊻; ↔ for ≡.
Define problems in Boolean logic by turning conditions into variables: for example, "the alarm sounds if the door is open and the system is armed, or the panic button is pressed" becomes (D ∧ A) ∨ P.
Convert between Boolean expressions, logic gate diagrams and truth tables in any direction. A truth table with n inputs has 2^n rows; working through intermediate columns avoids mistakes.

Karnaugh maps: label rows and columns in Gray code order (00, 01, 11, 10), fill in the outputs, then group the 1s in rectangles of 1, 2, 4 or 8, as large as possible. Groups can overlap and wrap around the edges. Each group gives one term, made of the variables that stay the same throughout it.
Rules for simplifying: De Morgan's laws, distribution, association, commutation and double negation. Show each step when you use them.
key_points.code:
De Morgan:      ¬(A ∧ B) ≡ ¬A ∨ ¬B      ¬(A ∨ B) ≡ ¬A ∧ ¬B
Distribution:   A ∧ (B ∨ C) ≡ (A ∧ B) ∨ (A ∧ C)
                A ∨ (B ∧ C) ≡ (A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ C)
Association:    (A ∧ B) ∧ C ≡ A ∧ (B ∧ C)
Commutation:    A ∧ B ≡ B ∧ A
Double negation: ¬¬A ≡ A

key_points.text: A D-type flip-flop stores one bit. When the clock pulse rises, the output (Q) takes the value of the data input (D); between pulses it holds that value whatever D does. Flip-flops are used to build registers and memory. You don't need to memorise the gates inside it.
A half adder adds two bits: Sum = A ⊻ B, Carry = A ∧ B. It can't take a carry in, so it can only add the least significant bits.

A full adder adds A, B and a carry in: Sum = A ⊻ B ⊻ Cin, Carry out = (A ∧ B) ∨ (Cin ∧ (A ⊻ B)). It can be built from two half adders and an OR gate, and full adders are chained (carry out to carry in) to add whole binary numbers.

dont_confuse.text: OR vs XOR: OR is true if either or both inputs are true; XOR is true only if exactly one is.
Half vs full adder: a half adder has two inputs (no carry in); a full adder has three (including carry in).
Association vs commutation: association regroups brackets; commutation swaps the order of inputs.
Karnaugh map order: columns go 00, 01, 11, 10 (Gray code), not 00, 01, 10, 11, so neighbouring cells differ by one bit.
